title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
authors: Angelopoulou, E.; Gandhi, K.; van Wolfswinkel, M.; Schmautz, L.; Oyarzun, I.; Nowosadtko, S.; Fischer, I.; Schwartz, V.; Griss, J. J.; Ellis, S. J.
abstract: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.

title: Gene-level evolutionary conservation and human constraint decline at comparable rates across the age of onset of Mendelian disease
authors: Mahaboob Ali, A. A.; Nelson, E. J. R.
abstract: Background Gene-level constraint and conservation scores are widely used to prioritise disease genes and to benchmark genomic language models. Purifying selection acts weakly on phenotypes manifesting after reproduction, so these scores are expected to carry less information about late-onset disease. An onset-dependent gradient has been demonstrated for human allele frequencies but not for the gene-level scores used in practice. Results We built an age-of-onset axis for 2,885 Mendelian diseases from Orphanet and fitted cross-species conservation (241-way phyloP) and human-population constraint (shet) on the same 5,322 gene-disease pairs against matched controls, to test whether one decays faster with onset. Their onset slopes differed by 0.23 logit units (97.5% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.56), equivalent to 0.024 units of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in a design resolving 0.049; the interval excludes constraint losing discriminative power faster than conservation by more than 0.011 AUROC units, widening to 0.033 when somatic associations are dropped. The usual explanation, that early-onset disease genes are developmental, pleiotropic and haploinsufficient by construction, did not account for the contrast; conditioning barely moved it. The answer did, however, depend on the constraint metric: three alternatives yielded larger contrasts excluding zero, though paired comparison could not distinguish the estimates. The metrics also diverged on recessive disease genes, with shet ranked below the gene pool (AUROC 0.487) and loss-of-function depletion above it (0.533), though, against matched controls, both ranked them below (0.457 and 0.450). Evolutionary scores improved a non-evolutionary baseline by 17 to 23%, with no onset gradient. Conclusions Conservation and constraint do not lose their value at measurably different rates as disease onset rises, and with only 283 late-onset Mendelian diseases annotated genome-wide, the question cannot be settled more finely. The gene-class explanation does not account for the contrast. Metrics that rank genes near-identically can still yield opposite onset-stratified answers, so a result reported by one metric carries a sensitivity that its confidence interval does not show. No constraint metric identifies recessive disease genes against matched controls, so a pipeline with recessive disease in scope needs a correction that switching metric does not supply.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the chilli thrips Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae)
authors: Busuulwa, A.; Liesenfelt, T.; Mongue, A. J.; Lahiri, S.
abstract: Thrips are known for being pests of many agricultural crops, as well as vectors of plant viruses. Yet despite their economic importance, genomic resources for this group remain limited, and no chromosome-level genome has been available for the genus Scirtothrips. One such species is the chilli thrips, Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae). This invasive and highly polyphagous pest is established across much of the world and transmits several tospoviruses. Genomic resources would provide a new means to understand the traits that make thrips difficult to manage. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly for S. dorsalis. The assembly is 266.5 Mb, with 96.9% of the sequence anchored in 16 chromosome-scale scaffolds. It contains 20,557 genes, and repetitive elements account for 28.8% of the sequence, which is comparable to those of other sequenced Thripidae. A species tree based on 3,019 single copy orthologs placed S. dorsalis as sister to Scirtothrips hansoni, with Scirtothrips most closely related to Frankliniella, Megalurothrips, and Odontothrips. The mitochondrial genome is a single circular molecule of 15,207 bp in which the sequence of the published mini circle is integrated, in contrast to the bipartite mitogenome previously reported for the same cryptic species.

title: Protein Language Model-Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Multitask Ligand Activity Prediction Across Human GPCRs
authors: De, M.; Lodh, E.; Majumder, S.; Chowdhury, T.
abstract: Predicting ligand activity across G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) requires models that capture both molecular structure and receptor-specific information while remaining robust to chemical and target-domain shifts. We developed a multimodal graph neural network that combines explicit ligand molecular graphs with frozen protein language model representations of GPCR sequences and jointly predicts quantitative pActivity and binary activity. The model was trained on 271,739 curated ligand-GPCR pairs spanning 183,694 ligands and 216 human GPCRs and evaluated using random, Bemis-Murcko scaffold, and strict cold-ligand partitions. With ESM-2 650M receptor embeddings, the selected model achieved mean absolute errors of 0.513 {+/-} 0.006, 0.540 {+/-} 0.006, and 0.641 {+/-} 0.005 pActivity units under random, cold-ligand, and scaffold evaluation, respectively, substantially outperforming a protein-aware fixed-feature multilayer perceptron and consistently improving quantitative prediction over a matched GINE reference. Removing receptor embeddings markedly degraded both regression and classification, whereas differences among ESM-2 35M, ESM-2 650M, and ProtT5 were comparatively small. Independent evaluation on 6,319 ChEMBL 37/BindingDB pairs revealed a substantial external domain shift, with mean absolute error increasing to approximately 0.94-0.95 despite chemically stringent internal validation. Nevertheless, receptor-specific information remained highly informative in a DRD2-DRD3 selectivity analysis: the cold-ligand ensemble achieved R^2 = 0.853, Spearman {rho} = 0.916, and ROC-AUC = 0.966 for strong DRD3 selectivity, whereas the receptor-independent ablation approached chance-level discrimination. These results establish protein-language-model-conditioned molecular graph learning as a scalable strategy for GPCR bioactivity prediction while identifying chemotype novelty, external-domain transfer, and richer ligand-receptor interaction representations as key remaining challenges.

title: CSF1R inhibition during cranial radiotherapy reshapes the immune environment and glial dynamics
authors: Leter, Y. M.; van Heijningen, C. L.; Tolboom, Z. J.; de Gooijer, M. C.; Compter, A.; van Tellingen, O.; Schagen, S. B.; Kuil, L. E.
abstract: Background: Cranial radiotherapy (cRT) induces long-lasting alterations in the brain microenvironment, including changes in glial populations and loss of neurogenesis. Pharmacological depletion of microglia via colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibition has been proposed as a strategy to modulate radiation-induced neuroinflammation, but its effects on other glial populations remains incompletely understood. Methods: Nine-week-old male C57BL/6JRj mice (n=60) received either a CSF1R-inhibitor supplemented diet (pexidartinib, PLX3397) or a control diet prior to and continued for 10 days after fractionated CT-guided cRT (3x10 Gy, 30 Gy). Brain tissue was assessed at multiple time-points up to six months post cRT using immunohistochemistry for markers of microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and proliferating cells. Microglial identity and repopulation dynamics were assessed using IBA1, F4/80 and the homeostatic microglial marker P2RY12, complemented by morphometric analysis. Results: Pexidartinib alone resulted in partial microglial depletion, whereas its combination with cRT led to near-complete loss of P2RY12+ homeostatic microglia at early time points. After discontinuation of the diet this was accompanied by increased IBA1+;F4/80high;P2RY12neg cell densities, consistent with replacement of the microglial niche by monocyte-derived cells. Over time, these cells exhibited gradual morphological adaptation but remained largely P2RY12neg, indicating incomplete restoration of a homeostatic microglial phenotype. Combined treatment accelerated astrocytic reactivity compared to cRT alone and did not prevent cRT-induced loss of neurogenesis or OPCs. At later time points, partial OPC recovery was observed in selected regions in the combined treatment group. Conclusion: CSF1R inhibition during cRT profoundly alters the composition and temporal dynamics of the brain its myeloid compartment, characterized by sustained loss of homeostatic microglia and replacement by monocyte-derived cells. Under these experimental conditions, microglial depletion did not mitigate key histopathological features associated with radiation-induced brain injury and was associated with accelerated astrocytic responses. These findings highlight the importance of timing, extent of depletion, and repopulation dynamics when considering microglia-targeting strategies in the context of cranial radiotherapy.

title: Evidence-Gated Plasticity and Context-Dependent Consolidation for Multi-Goal Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
authors: Neymotin, S. A.; Hazan, H.; Unal, G.; Earl, C.; Anwar, H.; Franaszczuk, P.; Boothe, D.
abstract: Background / Introduction: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks offer a mechanistic framework for adaptive behavior, yet learning multiple goals remains challenging when synaptic updates for different targets interfere. We investigated whether multi-timescale plasticity and context-specific credit assignment improve interleaved multi-goal learning in a spiking navigation system inspired by entorhinal-hippocampal circuitry. Methods: We introduce evidence-gated plasticity (EGP), in which reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) generates transient synaptic proposals and need-weighted behavioral evidence modulates their slower consolidation into durable weights. Global EGP pools these proposals and the corresponding evidence across goals. Target-context EGP extends this framework through goal-specific proposal and evidence stores and additional need-dependent scaling of consolidation. We compared the algorithms across paired spiking networks, tested learned weights with plasticity disabled, and examined upstream representations and consolidation components. Results: Global EGP supported multi-goal learning and durable navigation. Target-context EGP improved early reward across 40 paired networks, including an independently specified 30-pair replication. Across eight paired networks trained for 2000 episodes, target-context EGP maintained a reward advantage, increased target-contact success, and reduced expected time to reach the target when unsuccessful blocks were included. Independent fixed-weight evaluation demonstrated durable navigation in both algorithms, with seven of eight networks favoring target-context EGP. A component experiment reproduced the target-context reward advantage and identified additional need-dependent scaling of context-specific consolidation as the only component with adjusted statistical support for improved reward. Conclusions: EGP supports durable multi-goal learning in spiking neural networks, and its target-context extension improves acquisition and conditional target selectivity in this interleaved navigation task. The framework offers a basis for testing context-sensitive, evidence-modulated plasticity in other multi-context learning problems.

title: Hunger reconfigures a reward learning circuit into a memory competent mode
authors: Park, A.; Senapati, B.; Mancini, N.; Zhang, Y.; Choi, J.; Cone, I.; Treiber, C. D.; Costa, R. P.; Fenk, L. M.; Bidaye, S. S.; Waddell, S.
abstract: Internal states such as hunger dynamically reshape activity across circuits to support resource seeking. Neuromodulation provides a means of controlling such physiological properties of neurons, but how this flexibility regulates memory networks remains unclear. Here, we describe how hunger reconfigures a dopaminergic food-reward circuit between two physiological modes that support memory formation, in Drosophila. Starvation suppresses baseline dopaminergic activity through peptidergic signalling, enabling reward-evoked, large-amplitude dopamine neuron spikes to reinforce learning. This spiking mode can be engaged by sugar consumption and persists beyond feeding, reflecting the fly's satiety state. Persistent dopaminergic large-amplitude spiking reinforces learning and transitions the memory network into a mode that prioritizes consolidation of recently acquired memories. The transition from hunger to satiation is also reflected in the activity of postsynaptic output neurons that shift from a tonic, decorrelated mode that is responsive to dopamine into a bursting, correlated mode in which further dopaminergic modulation is occluded. Therefore, nutrient deprivation reconfigures the memory circuit into a learning competent dopamine-receptive mode, which persistent reinforcing dopamine then switches into a satiated mode driving memory consolidation. Together these processes mechanistically intertwine state-dependent reward-signalling with subsequent memory stabilization through transitions in physiological mode.

title: Sequence-Dependent DNA Base Selection Fidelity: A Kinetics-Based Model and its Validation
authors: Ghosh, K.; Sahu, P.; Barik, S.; Subramanian, H.
abstract: DNA replication achieves error rates as low as 10-9-10-11 per base pair through the combined contribution of base selection, exonuclease proofreading, and mismatch repair. Among those processes, base selection determines the initial level of accuracy and is strongly modulated by local sequence context. Existing models address this dependence either by fitting individual rate constants for each sequence context or by invoking the global template properties, neither of which derives sequence dependence from the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics of base pair formation. Here we present a mechanism for sequence-dependent base selection fidelity, built from two physical properties: nearest-neighbor stacking thermodynamics and directional kinetic asymmetry. The model fits the experimentally observed mutation spectra from three mismatch repair-deficient organisms well (r=0.74, 0.70, and 0.63), and predicts that base-selection accuracy varies non-monotonically with temperature in a sequence-dependent manner. Our model, therefore, provides a framework that connects sequence-dependent thermodynamic and kinetic effects during nucleotide incorporation to experimentally observed mutation rates.

title: EventHorizon: A Foundation Model for Clinical Flow Cytometry
authors: Medina Grespan, M.; Morrison, M.; O'Fallon, B.; Jacobsen, J. R.; Shean, R. C.; Spies, N. C.; Ng, D.
abstract: Clinical flow cytometry is central to diagnosing hematologic malignancies, but its reliance on manual expert interpretation and fixed panel designs limits scalability and adaptability. To address this, we developed EventHorizon, a self-supervised foundation model that combines a hierarchical, marker-aware transformer with self-distillation pre-training. EventHorizon integrates heterogeneous, multi-tube panels into a unified, specimen-level embedding. Pre-trained without labels on 100,937 routine clinical specimens, comprising over 50 billion cells, the model yields frozen embeddings that enable lightweight classifiers to accurately identify recurrent genetic abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including t(15;17) (AUROC 0.991) and an unexpected signal for DDX41 mutations (AUROC 0.970). EventHorizon maintained strong performance on a temporally separated 2026 cohort (macro AUROC 0.970 across 28 diagnoses) and demonstrated zero-shot transferability across a five-site B-cell lymphoma cohort (CLL vs. normal AUROC 0.988), the FlowCAP-II AML challenge (AUROC 0.973), and B-ALL measurable residual disease detection (AUROC 0.920 at [≥]1% disease burden). Although class ranking transferred reliably across sites, decision thresholds shifted; however, these were rapidly recalibrated using as few as four labeled AML cases. Sensitivity decreased at disease burdens below 0.1%, yet embeddings remained robust to simulated assay perturbations. Overall, EventHorizon offers a reusable, panel-agnostic representation for diagnostic flow cytometry.

title: The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
authors: Feathers, J. R.; Heeter, R.; Woollard, G.; Hanson, S. M.; Cossio, P.; Greer, J.; Burnley, T.; Zhong, E.
abstract: The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.

title: The dentate gyrus controls hippocampal representational drift
authors: GoodSmith, D.; Madar, A.; Carson, W. H.; Sheffield, M. E.
abstract: Neural representations evolve across time and experience, a phenomenon termed representational drift. The function and circuit mechanisms of drift remain unknown, including whether it reflects intrinsic biological variability within the population or is actively controlled by circuit inputs. Progress has been limited because there is currently no known experimental means to manipulate drift without also altering an animal's sensory or behavioral experience. Here we show that drift can be experimentally controlled through targeted manipulation of upstream circuit inputs. We demonstrate this principle in the hippocampus by selectively manipulating dentate gyrus granule cells, which are thought to promote discrimination between similar experiences. Inhibiting granule cells during repeated experiences in familiar virtual environments markedly reduced drift in downstream CA1, revealing that representational drift is not simply an intrinsic property of neural populations, but is actively controlled by upstream circuitry. By experimentally manipulating this circuit-level control of drift, we further discovered that hippocampal drift is concentrated around episode transitions rather than accumulating continuously throughout an experience. These findings establish experimental control over hippocampal drift, revealing a structured, circuit-regulated process that differentiates repeated experiences into distinct episodic representations.
